name: Cialdini's Influence Principles
origin: Robert Cialdini's influence principles, drawn from experimental social psychology. This drill is an original training adaptation of the published principles.
evidenceType: Experimental social psychology. Individual effects are well studied, though some classic findings have replicated with smaller effects than first reported.
fits: Ethical nudges toward a decision the buyer already wants
strains: Skeptical buyers who spot technique quickly
Any use where the principle is faked (fake scarcity, fake social proof)
coreMoves: Reciprocity: give something genuinely useful first (an insight, a benchmark, a free audit) with no strings.
Commitment and consistency: get small, voluntary, sincere agreements that line up with the buyer's own stated goals.
Social proof: cite real, comparable customers and real results, including the typical result, not only the best one.
Authority: show relevant expertise and credentials honestly; let evidence carry the weight.
Liking: find real common ground and be genuinely helpful; do not fake rapport.
Scarcity: mention real limits (real deadlines, real capacity) only when they exist.

opener: Built genuine liking or gave something of value early
discovery: Learned what the buyer values so the principles could be applied honestly
Secured small, sincere agreements tied to the buyer's own goals
objectionHandling: Used real, comparable social proof to answer doubts
Did not escalate to pressure or fake urgency
close: Anchored and traded deliberately in negotiation (give something only to get something)
Used silence and clear asks rather than filling space with concessions
Any scarcity or deadline mentioned was real

ethicsGuardrails: Fake scarcity, invented deadlines and made-up customer stories are deception and must be flagged.
Reciprocity must not be used to create guilt.
The buyer in this app is told to call out manipulative use.
